title: Fixed-Term Employment Contracts in India: Rights, Limits and Open Questions
meta_description: What fixed-term employment means under the Industrial Relations Code, how it differs from probation and contract labour, and what is unsettled on gratuity.
intro: A fixed-term employment contract hires a worker directly by the employer for a defined period, with a start date and an end date written into the contract itself. It sits apart from probation, which is a trial phase inside an otherwise open-ended job, and from contract labour, where workers are supplied by a separate contractor or staffing agency rather than hired directly. The four Labour Codes, in force since 21 November 2025, give fixed-term employment formal, direct recognition for the first time across all sectors, and that recognition brings specific rights that an employer cannot contract around.

sections.heading: What counts as fixed-term employment
paragraphs: Under the Industrial Relations Code, fixed-term employment means engaging a worker through a written contract for a defined period, where the job ends on its own when that period expires, without the employer needing to retrench the worker or follow the usual termination process that applies to open-ended employment. The written contract is not optional. A verbal understanding that a job will last roughly a year, or an appointment letter that is silent on an end date, does not create fixed-term employment; it risks being treated as ordinary permanent employment with no fixed end point, which carries a very different set of obligations when the employer eventually wants to end it.

Fixed-term employment is available across industries and roles, including for project-based work, seasonal work, replacement of an employee on leave, or a defined engagement tied to a client contract. It differs from a probationer, who is a new permanent employee under assessment, and from an apprentice, who is undergoing training under a separate apprenticeship framework. It also differs from contract labour supplied through a staffing agency or contractor, where the principal employer does not have a direct employment relationship with the worker at all.

sections.heading: The parity rule
paragraphs: The core protection written into the Industrial Relations Code is parity. A fixed-term employee doing the same or similar work as a permanent employee is entitled to the same hours of work, wages, allowances and other statutory benefits as that permanent employee. An employer cannot use a fixed-term label to pay a lower rate for identical work, or to withhold facilities ordinarily extended to permanent staff doing the same job on the same floor.

This parity requirement is the main reason fixed-term employment is not simply a cheaper substitute for contract labour. A business that wants to reduce labour cost below what a permanent employee would earn for the same role needs a genuinely different arrangement, such as outsourcing the function to a contractor, rather than dressing up the same role as fixed-term and paying less for it. A worker who believes parity has been denied can raise the point with the employer's grievance mechanism in the first instance, and ultimately before the labour authorities, by pointing to what a comparable permanent employee in the same establishment actually receives for the same work.

sections.heading: Gratuity: the one-year question
paragraphs: Ordinarily, gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act requires five years of continuous service before it becomes payable. For fixed-term employees, commentary following the Labour Codes has consistently read the law as reducing this to a one-year qualifying period, so that a fixed-term worker who completes a full year on a fixed-term contract becomes entitled to gratuity calculated on a pro-rata basis for the period actually served, even where the overall contract itself runs for only that one year.

Exactly where this one-year rule is anchored in the statute is less settled than the outcome itself. Some analyses place the reduced threshold in the Code on Social Security, 2020; others point instead to the Industrial Relations Code and treat the Code on Social Security's own text as not spelling out the one-year figure directly, leaving it to draft central rules to fill the gap. For an employer or employee relying on this, the safer course is to check the central rules actually notified for the Code on Social Security at the time a particular contract is signed, rather than assuming the one-year figure is beyond dispute, since practitioner commentary itself is divided on its precise statutory source.

sections.heading: What happens when the contract ends
paragraphs: A fixed-term contract that simply runs its course and ends on the agreed date is not a retrenchment, and the elaborate notice, compensation and government-permission requirements that apply to retrenching a permanent workman under the Industrial Relations Code do not apply in the same way to a fixed-term contract reaching its natural end. This is one of the main reasons employers use fixed-term contracts for defined projects or seasonal peaks, since it avoids the retrenchment process for work that was never intended to be permanent.

This flexibility has a limit that employers in Delhi NCR and Kolkata should treat carefully. Repeatedly renewing a series of short fixed-term contracts for what is, in substance, a permanent and continuous role invites the risk that a labour court or industrial tribunal treats the arrangement as a disguised permanent appointment, with the fixed-term label used only to avoid retrenchment protections. Courts have historically looked past form to substance in this kind of dispute, and nothing in the new Codes removes that scrutiny.

sections.heading: Statutory benefits beyond gratuity
paragraphs: Fixed-term employees are generally brought within the Employees' Provident Fund and Employees' State Insurance frameworks on the same basis as permanent employees once the usual wage and establishment-size thresholds are met, since these schemes turn on the employment relationship and wage level rather than on whether the contract has a fixed end date. Leave entitlements, weekly rest and working-hour limits likewise apply on the same statutory basis as for permanent staff, consistent with the broader parity principle.

Where a fixed-term employee's contract is for less than a full year, the position on gratuity is more restrictive. Commentary generally treats a contract period of under one year as falling outside the pro-rata gratuity benefit altogether, since the one-year figure functions as a qualifying period, not merely a basis for proportionate calculation. An employer structuring a series of short-term engagements under a year each should expect this distinction to be scrutinised if the arrangement is later challenged.

sections.heading: Drafting the contract
paragraphs: A fixed-term contract should state the start date, the end date or the specific event that ends the engagement, the role and reporting line, and the wages, allowances and benefits being offered, cross-checked against what a permanent employee in a comparable role receives. It should also state clearly that the engagement ends automatically on the stated date without any further notice being required, since an ambiguous contract gives an aggrieved employee room to argue that ordinary termination protections should have applied.

Employers who want the option to renew should say so expressly and should keep a genuine business reason on file for each renewal, whether that is an extended project timeline, continued seasonal demand, or a client contract that itself got extended. A documented reason for each renewal is the single most useful protection against a later claim that the fixed-term structure was used only to deny permanent status, and it also gives the employer a clear record to produce if a dispute ever reaches a labour court.

faqs.q: Can a fixed-term employee be dismissed before the contract period ends?
faqs.a: Yes, but not without cause. Ending a fixed-term contract early, before its stated end date, is a termination and is generally treated like ending any other employment relationship early, meaning the usual contractual notice or termination provisions and any applicable statutory protections against unfair termination can apply. The automatic, notice-free end on the agreed date is available only when the contract actually runs its full term.

faqs.q: Does a fixed-term employee get the same leave as a permanent employee?
faqs.a: Generally yes, on a proportionate basis tied to the length of service, since statutory leave entitlements are not conditioned on permanent status. The specific number of days and carry-forward rules depend on the applicable state shops and establishments rules or the relevant central rules for the sector.

faqs.q: Can an employer keep renewing fixed-term contracts indefinitely for the same role?
faqs.a: There is no fixed statutory cap on the number of renewals stated in the Codes themselves, but repeated renewal for what is functionally a permanent, continuous role risks being treated by a labour court as a disguised permanent appointment. Each renewal should have a genuine, documented business reason.

faqs.q: Is a fixed-term employee entitled to provident fund contributions?
faqs.a: Generally yes, once the establishment and wage thresholds under the Employees' Provident Funds Act (or the corresponding provisions carried into the Code on Social Security) are met, since coverage turns on the employment relationship and wages, not on whether the contract has a fixed end date.

faqs.q: What is the single biggest risk for an employer using fixed-term contracts?
faqs.a: Treating a fixed-term label as a way to pay less than a comparable permanent employee for the same work, or to avoid retrenchment protections for a role that is, in substance, permanent. Both invite challenge, the first under the Code's parity rule, the second under the long-standing judicial practice of looking at substance over form in employment disputes.

references: Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 (as continued under the Code on Social Security, 2020)
Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 (as continued under the Code on Social Security, 2020)
verification_notes: Chosen because the four Labour Codes (in force from 21 November 2025) are an explicit current-law reference point for this run, and the site's existing labour-code guides cover the Codes generally and retrenchment specifically but do not have a dedicated practical guide to fixed-term employment, confirmed by a site search showing zero existing items on 'fixed term employment', 'probation period' or 'employment bond'. The parity rule and the one-year-service figure for gratuity are reported consistently across multiple law-firm sources (ksandk.com, Bhatt & Joshi Associates, a CNLU paper), but the precise statutory provision anchoring the one-year gratuity threshold is genuinely disputed in the sources themselves (some citing the Code on Social Security, others the Industrial Relations Code and draft central rules), and this guide states that disagreement openly rather than picking one source and presenting it as settled. No case law, figures or dates are asserted beyond what the sources support; readers are pointed to check the actual notified central rules at the time of contracting.
